title: Diffuse co-expression of TTF-1 and p40 (ΔNp63) defines a distinct biphenotypic non-small cell lung carcinoma: clinicopathologic and molecular characterization of 19 cases
author: Jielu Lin; Shaoling Li; Weijie Chen; Wei Wu; Wei Zhang; Yan Huang; Zhengwei Dong; Chunyan Wu; Likun Hou
text:
Abstract
Background
The diffuse co-expression of thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and p40 defines a rare and diagnostically challenging subtype of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). Due to its extreme rarity, the clinicopathologic and molecular characteristics of this entity remain poorly characterized.
Methods
We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the largest single-institution cohort to date (n = 19) of NSCLCs with diffuse TTF-1/p40 co-expression. All cases underwent detailed histopathologic review. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) utilized specific antibody clones (TTF-1: 8G7G3/1; p40). Molecular profiling was performed via next-generation sequencing in a subset of cases, including multi-region analysis for select tumors.
Results
The cohort mainly consisted of elderly male smokers (median age 65; 84.2% male; 73.7% smokers). Anatomically, 84.2% of tumors were located in the right lung, mainly in the upper lobe, with no clear preference for central or peripheral distribution. Histologically, all were poorly differentiated NSCLCs, classifiable into two patterns: a basaloid/squamous-like pattern and an inflammatory/plasmacytoid pattern. Molecular profiling revealed a hybrid genomic landscape, with individual tumors harboring alterations linked to both adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, along with a high prevalence(58.8%) of TP53 mutations. In an index case, multi-region sequencing revealed a shared EGFR mutation across regions, with a TP53 mutation confined to the high-grade TTF-1/p40-positive area. Most patients (66.7%) presented with Stage III or IV disease, and 61.1% developed metastases, including four with distant spread and seven involving thoracic or supraclavicular lymph nodes or the pleura. Three patients died from the disease within 10–64 months after diagnosis. However, all patients with Stage I or II disease who underwent resection remained disease-free.
Conclusions
NSCLC with diffuse TTF-1/p40 co-expression constitutes a distinct biphenotypic entity with unique clinicopathologic and molecular features. We suggest specific diagnostic criteria to ensure proper identification. Given the presence of targetable drivers and frequent PD-L1 expression, an integrated diagnostic approach is crucial for guiding personalized therapy and enhancing patient outcomes.
Keywords: Non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), TTF-1, p40, biphenotypic, immunohistochemistry, next-generation sequencing, molecular profiling, targeted therapy
Introduction
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, with non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) making up about 85% of cases [1]. The main histological subtypes are adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC). Accurate pathological classification of NSCLC is crucial, as it informs initial treatment selection and guides decisions regarding molecular testing [2].
Standard diagnostic practice relies on immunohistochemical markers. Thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and p40 (ΔNp63) are lineage-specific markers that typically show mutually exclusive expression [3]. Diffuse co-expression of TTF-1 and p40 in a single NSCLC is rare. This immunophenotype does not fit standard diagnostic categories, challenging the binary approach and risking clinical delays. Since its first description in 2015 [4], fewer than 40 such cases have been reported in the literature, primarily as individual case reports [5–11] or several series [12–15]. The diagnostic criteria and molecular understanding of this phenotype remain poorly defined due to fragmented data and limited high-quality tissue for comprehensive analysis. To address this, we present the largest single-institution cohort (n = 19) of these dual-positive tumors. A key strength of our series is the predominance of surgical resection specimens (10/19), allowing thorough histologic and multi-region molecular analysis. Through this comprehensive approach, we seek to definitively characterize this challenging entity and clarify its clinicopathologic and biological significance.
Patients and Methods
Patients and Diagnostic Criteria
The Institutional Review Board of Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital approved this retrospective study. We searched our institution’s pathology archival database for cases of poorly differentiated NSCLC diagnosed from January 2017 to September 2024. Initial screening identified tumors reported to express both TTF-1 and p40 by immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis. Clinical and demographic data were extracted from electronic medical records.
The diagnosis of poorly differentiated NSCLC with actual co-expression of TTF-1 and p40 was thoroughly confirmed using the following criteria:
-
i.
Morphological Criteria: Histological evidence of poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma, with no morphological signs of adenocarcinoma (e.g., gland formation) or squamous differentiation (e.g., keratin pearls, intercellular bridges), as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) [2];
-
ii.
Immunohistochemical Criteria: Immunohistochemical analysis showing diffuse (≥ 50% of tumor cells) and strong (intensity score of 3 + on a scale of 0–3) nuclear positivity for TTF-1 and p40 within the same tumor cells;
-
iii.
Exclusion Criteria: Excluding adeno-squamous carcinomas with two distinct components, as well as tumors where TTF-1 and p40 are expressed in separate cells or areas.
All hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides (H&E), as well as IHC and special stains, were independently reviewed by two experienced pulmonary pathologists to confirm the diagnosis according to the criteria above. Any discrepant cases were discussed under a multi-head microscope to reach a consensus.
A total of 19 cases met all criteria and were included in the final cohort, comprising nine biopsy samples and ten surgical resection specimens.
Immunohistochemistry
Immunohistochemistry was performed on 4-µm FFPE sections using an automated stainer (Aliya-B4, Talent Biomedical, Xiamen, China). After antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0), sections were incubated with antibodies against TTF-1 (mouse monoclonal, clone 8G7G6/1; Dako; 1:300) and p40 (rabbit polyclonal; ZSbio; 1:200), followed by HRP-polymer detection (Dako K5007) with DAB chromogen. All batches included positive and negative controls.
Double immunofluorescence
Consecutive FFPE sections were processed for double IF using the same dewaxing and antigen retrieval protocol as IHC. Sections were co-incubated with primary antibodies (TTF-1, Dako, 1:300; p40, ZSbio, 1:200), followed by a mixture of secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488 anti-rabbit and Alexa Fluor 594 anti-mouse, YEASEN). Nuclei were stained with DAPI. Images were captured with a fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX53) and merged using ImageJ.
Molecular Analysis
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) or targeted PCR was attempted for all 19 cases. Adequate nucleic acids for analysis were obtained from 17 cases. Twelve cases underwent comprehensive profiling using large NGS panels (GENESEEQ PRIMETM, GENESEEQ Inc.), which covered either 425 or 2000 cancer-related genes. This included core lung cancer driver genes (e.g., EGFR, ALK, ROS1) and a broad spectrum of other clinically relevant genes, including BRAF, MET, RET, ERBB2, KRAS, NRAS, TP53, and MYC. In Case 15, which exhibited a lepidic adenocarcinoma component distinct from the TTF-1/p40-coexpressing NSCLC, the two histologically distinct regions were separately microdissected before NGS. The remaining five profiled cases were evaluated using amplification refractory mutation system (ARMS)-PCR, with either a targeted nine-gene panel (covering EGFR, KRAS, BRAF, ALK, ROS1, RET, NRAS, ERBB2, and MET exon 14 skipping) (n = 4) or single-gene EGFR testing (n = 1). The two remaining cases lacked sufficient quality or quantity of nucleic acids for reliable analysis.
Results
Clinical features
Table 1 summarizes the clinical features of 19 patients with NSCLC co-expressing TTF1 and p40. The cohort included 10 surgical and 9 biopsy specimens, comprising 16 males and 3 females, with a median age of 65 years (range 43–78). Most patients (14/19, 73.7%) had a smoking history. Tumor sizes ranged from 10 mm to 97 mm (mean 52 mm). The majority of tumors (16/19, 84.2%) were located in the right lung, with the right upper lobe being the most frequent site (5/19, 26.3%). Tumors were classified as central type in 10 cases and peripheral type in 9 cases. Among the 18 patients with available TNM staging, 66.7% (12/18) presented with advanced disease (Stages III/IV), while the remaining 33.3% (6/18) were at Stages I-II. Most patients (17/19, 89.5%) exhibited nonspecific symptoms, such as cough, hemoptysis, or chest pain; two were asymptomatic and had pulmonary nodules incidentally discovered during routine imaging.

Pathologic Findings
All 19 cases were classified as poorly differentiated NSCLCs. Six cases (32%) showed basaloid features, including small to medium-sized cells, scant eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, a high mitotic index, and a solid, expansive growth pattern with peripheral palisading and extensive necrosis (Fig. 1). The remaining 13 cases consisted of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and frequent mitotic figures. Scattered necrosis was found in three cases, and five cases had inflammatory infiltrates (Fig. 2). These two distinct morphological patterns suggested a diagnosis of poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma or other rare subtypes, prompting further immunohistochemical investigation.
Further histological examination provided clues to the different origins of differentiation within the tumor spectrum. Tumor cells were seen migrating along the basal layer of the bronchiolar epithelium (Case #5, Fig. 3A). Focal lepidic growth adenocarcinoma was identified adjacent to the poorly differentiated NSCLC component in Case #15 (Figs. 3B-D).
Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the same tumor cells expressed both TTF-1 and p40. This co-localization within individual cells was clearly confirmed by double immunofluorescence (Fig. 4), indicating a unique dual-phenotype. Additional staining showed variable CK5/6 positivity (7/15 cases) but infrequent Napsin A reactivity (2/17 cases), supporting the abnormal differentiation state. Notably, PD-L1 expression was observed in 7/14 cases (50%), with a high TPS (≥ 50%) in 4 cases (28.6%).
Molecular Findings
Molecular profiling (17/19 cases) revealed a diverse yet informative genomic landscape (Table 2; Fig. 5). Putative driver alterations were found in 13 of 17 cases (76.5%), including classic adenocarcinoma-associated drivers such as EGFR mutations (5 cases), KRAS mutations (2 cases), and NKX2-1 amplification (1 case), along with alterations more common in squamous cell carcinoma, like FGFR3-TACC3 fusion, PIK3CA amplification, and CCNE1 amplification. The tumor suppressor gene TP53 was the most frequently altered (10 of 17 cases, 58.8%) and often co-occurred with other driver events. The EGFR variants identified included exon 19 deletions (n = 2), L858R (n = 1), and G719X (n = 1), while KRAS mutations were G12S and I36M. A strong correlation with smoking history was observed: five EGFR-mutant cases occurred in never-smokers (4 cases) and a long-term former smoker (1 case) who had abstained from smoking for 50 years, whereas KRAS and TP53 mutations were highly prevalent among current smokers.

Further mutation tests were conducted separately on the different histologic components of Case #15, which includes a mixed lepidic adenocarcinoma area and a TTF-1+/p40 + NSCLC area. The results are shown in Fig. 6. The EGFR p.E746_A750del mutation was detected in both components, with a comparatively higher variant allele frequency (VAF) in the lepidic adenocarcinoma area. Additionally, a pathogenic TP53 splice-site mutation (c.673–2 A > G) was identified exclusively in the TTF-1+/p40 + component, suggesting its acquisition contributed to the development of this distinct histologic phenotype.
Survival Outcomes and Follow-up Analysis
Clinical follow-up data were available for 18 of the 19 patients (94.7%). The median follow-up time for the entire group was 26 months (range, 10–88 months). Metastases occurred in 11 patients (11/18, 61.1%), including 4 with distant metastases and 7 with involvement of thoracic or supraclavicular lymph nodes or the pleura. Distant metastases were found in the brain, bones, adrenal glands, pericardium, and other sites. Three patients died from the disease 10 to 64 months after their initial diagnosis, while 15 remain alive, including five with no evidence of disease following primary tumor resection.
Discussion
A rare phenotype of poorly differentiated NSCLCs, with diffuse, concurrent co-expression of TTF-1 and p40, challenges the conventional binary classification and poses a diagnostic dilemma that can delay treatment decisions and molecular testing. Since Pelosi’s report in 2015 [4], reports of diffuse TTF-1 and p40 co-expression have remained extremely rare, limited to sporadic case reports and a few small case series [4–15]. Importantly, the variability in diagnostic methods and the lack of systematic molecular analysis across these studies have prevented a unified understanding of their biological drivers and clinical behavior. To fill these gaps, we have assembled, to our knowledge, the largest single-institution cohort of such cases (n = 19). A significant strength of this cohort is the high percentage of surgical resection specimens (10/19, 52.6%), which has provided the tissue quality and quantity needed for our comprehensive analysis. This includes detailed histologic reassessment and, as described in the Results section, multi-region genomic sequencing. Through this combined clinicopathologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular approach, we attempt to establish a definitive profile of this entity and investigate its cellular origins.
Clinically, our cohort of 19 patients, similar to previously reported studies (mean age: 68 years; predominantly male; 76.9% smokers) [4–15], was characterized by an elderly population with a median age of 65 years, a strong male dominance (84.2%), and a high rate of smoking history (73.7%). This consistency supports the link between this rare phenotype and populations that are elderly, male, and have a history of smoking, indicating possible shared etiological factors. While a prior study by Savari et al. highlighted a peripheral distribution [12], our data show no evident central or peripheral predilection. Moreover, we observed a significant right-sided predominance (84.2%), with the right upper lobe as the most frequent site. Prior dosimetry models indicated that cigarette smoke particles were preferentially deposited in the right upper lobe [16]. Although biological or exposure factors might influence this trend, larger multi-center studies are needed to confirm its significance and rule out sampling bias.
Histological examination confirmed that TTF-1/p40 co-expressing carcinomas are poorly differentiated NSCLCs. Based on both prior research and our analysis, we categorized these tumors into two patterns: a predominant basaloid/squamous-like pattern and an inflammatory/plasmacytoid pattern. The inflammatory/plasmacytoid pattern, seen in most of our cases (68%), features a prominent lymphoplasmacytic stroma. This histological feature suggests the presence of an immune-rich tumor microenvironment.
Several case reports and small series have examined PD-L1 expression in TTF1/p40 co-expressing non-small cell lung carcinomas. Among the 7 cases with explicitly reported PD-L1 results, 5 (75%) were positive: 3 exhibited high expression (≥ 50%), and 2 showed low/moderate expression (1 ~ 49%), while 2 cases (25%) were negative [11, 13, 14]. Savari et al. tested PD-L1 in their 14-case series but did not specify the number of positive cases or the exact expression levels in the provided content [12]. Our analysis found PD-L1 expression in 50% (7/14) of tested cases, with a high level (TPS ≥ 50%) in a notable subset (4/14). This prevalent PD-L1 positivity aligns with the dominant inflammatory/plasmacytoid morphological pattern observed in our cohort, characterized by a dense lymphoplasmacytic stroma. The observed co-occurrence of an inflammatory microenvironment and tumor PD-L1 expression could be explained by the adaptive immune resistance mechanism, wherein cytokines such as interferon-gamma, released by tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, induce PD-L1 upregulation in tumor cells [17].
While the co-expression of TTF-1 and p40 is a defining feature of this entity, diagnostic standardization—particularly regarding positivity thresholds and antibody clones—has not been standardized across studies. Current WHO guidelines classify TTF-1-positive tumors as adenocarcinoma (or “NSCLC favoring adenocarcinoma”) even with focal p40 expression, while adenosquamous carcinoma requires definitive biphasic morphology [2]. In the most extensive series to date (n = 14), Savari et al. (2023) pragmatically defined “diffuse co-expression” as positivity in 50–100% of tumor cells, a threshold that distinguishes this pattern from the scattered p40 positivity occasionally seen in adenocarcinomas [12]. While earlier case reports often lacked a specific numerical cutoff, descriptions such as “diffuse strong positivity” and supporting images consistently indicated that the majority of tumor cells (> 50%) expressed both markers. Antibody selection also varied, with the more specific TTF-1 clone 8G7G3/1 and p40 clone BC28 being most common, though some studies used fewer specific clones (e.g., TTF-1 SPT24) [6, 11]. Based on insights from the current cases, the following diagnostic criteria, aiming to ensure diagnostic reproducibility and biological distinctness from established WHO entities, are recommended: (i) Exclusion of other subtypes: Tumors composed of a single population of cells should be considered. Adenosquamous carcinomas with distinct components or tumors exhibiting separate regions of TTF-1 and p40 positivity should be excluded; (ii) Morphological features: The tumor should exhibit characteristics of poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma, without definitive morphological evidence of either squamous carcinoma or adenocarcinoma; (iii) Immunohistochemical profile: TTF-1 and p40 should show strong positivity in over 50% of the tumor cells, with a diffuse distribution within the same tumor cells. Preferential use of the more specific TTF-1 antibody (clone 8G7G3/1) is advised over SPT24 or SPT141 antibodies.
Our diagnostic criteria emphasize the use of highly specific antibodies, aligning with the majority of prior reports: p40 (to exclude 5% p63 diffuse positive adenocarcinomas [18, 19]) and TTF-1 clone 8G7G3/1 (to minimize cross-reactivity in squamous carcinomas, as associated with clones like SPT24) [20, 21].
Molecular profiling of TTF-1+/p40 + NSCLC reveals a hybrid genomic signature that challenges simple lineage classifications. Our findings show concurrent alterations associated with LUAD (e.g., EGFR, KRAS) and LUSC (e.g., FGFR3-TACC3, PIK3CA, CCNE1), along with frequent TP53 mutations. This hybrid profile mirrors the biphenotypic immunoprofile, reinforcing the concept of this tumor as a distinct entity. While previous studies reported high rates of FGFR pathway alterations (23.5%-70%) [12, 15], our cohort showed a lower prevalence (one FGFR3-TACC3 fusion), potentially reflecting cohort heterogeneity. However, our findings align with the literature regarding the high frequency of TP53 mutations (58.8%), suggesting that loss of this tumor suppressor is a critical and consistent event in tumor development. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between smoking history and mutation patterns: EGFR mutations were mainly found in never-smokers, while KRAS and TP53 alterations were more common in current smokers. This indicates that, while the immunophenotype is shared, the initiating molecular events may vary, further supporting biological uniqueness driven by diverse etiologic factors.
The histogenesis of TTF-1+/p40+ tumors remains a subject of debate, primarily centered on two hypotheses: a de novo origin from distal airway basal cells [7] versus lineage plasticity or transdifferentiation [12]. While Pelosi et al. identified a physiological subset of “TTF1/P40 double-positive stem-like basal cells” as a putative origin [7], Braun et al. recently proposed a mechanistic model in which TP53 mutations act as a key driver to deregulate p63/p40 expression in TTF-1-positive cells [15].
Our multi-region sequencing of Case #15 provides direct clinical evidence supporting this plasticity model. The identification of a shared EGFR p.E746_A750del mutation in both the lepidic adenocarcinoma component and the TTF-1+/p40 + NSCLC component confirms a common clonal origin, ruling out a collision tumor. Crucially, the subsequent acquisition of a pathogenic TP53 splice-site mutation (c.673–2 A > G) was exclusive to the high-grade TTF-1+/p40 + component. This finding suggests that TP53 inactivation functions as a pivotal “molecular switch,” where genomic instability and loss of checkpoint control promote lineage infidelity. This observation aligns robustly with the hypothesis by Braun et al. [15] and established cancer biology [22–24], implying that the distinct TTF-1+/p40 + phenotype in this case arose through subclonal evolution and cellular reprogramming of pre-existing adenocarcinoma cells, rather than solely from a de novo biphenotypic progenitor. This also mirrors the molecular mechanisms described in adenosquamous carcinoma, where TP53 and STK11/LKB1 inactivation are identified as critical drivers facilitating the reprogramming of adenocarcinoma cells toward a squamous phenotype [25, 26].
The clinical behavior of NSCLCs with diffuse TTF-1/p40 co-expression remains incompletely understood but indicates a generally aggressive course. Previous studies consistently describe these tumors as high-grade malignancies with a propensity for rapid progression. Savari et al. reported that 79% (11/14) of patients presented with nodal or distant metastases at the time of diagnosis [12]. Moreover, Braun et al. demonstrated that the poor prognosis in this subgroup is significantly associated with TP53 mutations and FGFR1 alterations [15]. In our cohort, this is shown by a high rate of advanced-stage disease at presentation (66.7%, Stages III/IV) and a significant rate of metastasis (61.1%). However, outcomes varied: five patients with early-stage disease remained disease-free after resection, highlighting the importance of disease stage and resectability. From a therapeutic perspective, the presence of targetable drivers (e.g., EGFR) and high PD-L1 expression (TPS ≥ 50% in 28.6%) has critical implications: the presence of diffuse p40 expression should not deter clinicians from ordering comprehensive molecular testing, as these patients may benefit significantly from targeted therapies or immunotherapy.
This study has several limitations. Despite comprising one of the largest single-institution cohorts to date, its retrospective nature and sample size preclude definitive generalizations. Additionally, the molecular associations observed, particularly the interplay between TP53 and phenotypic switching, require functional validation in experimental models. Future investigations should prioritize multi-institutional collaborations and employ single-cell or spatial transcriptomic technologies to further dissect the tumor heterogeneity and cellular origins of this rare entity.
Conclusion
In summary, TTF-1/p40 co-expressing NSCLC should be recognized as a distinct clinicopathologic entity characterized by poor differentiation, a unique dual immunophenotype, a complex molecular profile, and often aggressive behavior. We suggest diagnostic criteria that include a quantitative threshold for co-expression and specific recommendations for antibodies. To ensure effective patient management, an integrated diagnostic approach combining histology, validated IHC, mandatory NGS, and PD-L1 testing is essential. Identifying this entity is a vital step toward improving NSCLC classification and guiding targeted treatment strategies.
